strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: adapting visual information acquisition to the needs of high-level driving decisions. The integration of historical-view retrieval, cropping, depth estimation, and object detection provides a coherent tool-assisted reasoning framework.

The reported improvements are substantial. DriveAgent-R1 achieves 70.11% first-frame and 44.06% sequence-average scores, compared with 36.51% and 38.91% for the strongest prompted baseline on the respective metrics. Enabling tools also improves the trained model over its forced text-reasoning mode.

The training-stage ablations provide useful evidence: combining both RL stages improves performance over SFT alone and either individual RL stage. The paper clearly describes the overall architecture, data-construction pipeline, and reward components.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish state-of-the-art driving performance. Table 1 compares a task-trained model against one-shot general-purpose VLMs, without trained driving baselines such as an adapted AlphaDrive or a comparably trained action-prediction model. The no-tool baseline in Table 3 is useful, but does not isolate the proposed curriculum from conventional RL under matched training budgets.

The central efficiency and adaptive-selection claims lack direct evidence. There are no latency, token-cost, tool-frequency, or computation measurements. Free selection achieves 44.06% sequence accuracy versus 43.20% for always using tools, while first-frame accuracy decreases from 71.23% to 70.11%. Without uncertainty estimates or measured savings, the practical advantage is unclear. The 65.93% mode-selection accuracy also lacks constant-mode baselines and the distribution of optimal-mode labels.

The tool-use reward measures absolute prediction quality and tool-call validity, rather than whether tools improved the decision relative to reasoning without them. It can therefore reward unnecessary calls on already-solvable examples. No explicit computational cost is included, and reward-component ablations are missing. Consequently, the claimed learning of tool necessity is insufficiently supported.

Evaluation is limited to offline action prediction on one dataset with a custom random 1,500-sample test split. There is no cross-dataset evaluation, closed-loop assessment, or collision and traffic-rule evaluation. Predicting four coarse actions over eight seconds provides limited evidence of coherent long-horizon planning, and does not substantiate the conclusions about improved operational safety.

The evaluation metrics need stronger justification and specification. The reported accuracy includes partial credit for supposedly safer speed choices, despite initially being described as exact joint matching; slower actions are not universally safer. Strict accuracy and per-horizon results are absent. H-Score lacks the evaluator prompt, detailed rubric, normalization procedure, and human validation, limiting the interpretability of reasoning-quality claims.

Removing all images demonstrates sensitivity to visual input, but does not establish faithful grounding, resistance to textual shortcuts, or robustness. This intervention also disrupts the information required by the tools. Matched-information passive baselines, individual-tool ablations, and controlled visual counterfactuals are needed to distinguish active perception from access to additional resolution, history, and pretrained perception models.

Novelty and reproducibility remain insufficiently established. The method largely combines existing tool-augmented reasoning, mode routing, and GRPO; MP-GRPO is described primarily as forced sampling from both modes followed by pooled normalization. Its specific contribution is not isolated from additional training. Missing details include RL training lengths and learning rates, reward weights and curriculum thresholds, exploratory-set size, annotation prompts, and precise low-resolution versus retrieved-image settings. No repeated-run variability is reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: selectively acquiring additional visual evidence for high-level driving decisions. The integration of structured reasoning, visual tools, and adaptive mode selection is coherent.
Reported improvements on SUP-AD are substantial. DriveAgent-R1 achieves 70.11% first-frame and 44.06% sequence-average joint scores, compared with 36.22% and 38.91% for tool-enabled Gemini 2.5 Flash.

The training-stage ablations support the usefulness of the complete pipeline, and enabling tools improves the trained model over its forced text-reasoning mode. The paper also includes a useful baseline trained without tools.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish state-of-the-art driving performance. Table 1 compares a task-trained system against one-shot general-purpose VLMs, without evaluating relevant driving methods such as AlphaDrive or an appropriately adapted DriveVLM. The trained no-tool baseline helps, but matched-data, matched-compute comparisons are needed to isolate the proposed algorithmic contribution.

The central efficiency claim is untested. There are no latency, token-cost, tool-frequency, or accuracy–compute measurements. Always using tools achieves higher first-frame accuracy than adaptive selection (71.23% versus 70.11%), while its sequence score is only modestly lower (43.20% versus 44.06%). Without uncertainty estimates and measured savings, the benefit of adaptive selection remains unclear. The reported 65.93% mode-selection accuracy also lacks constant-mode baselines and the distribution of optimal modes.

The tool reward measures final accuracy and call validity rather than improvement attributable to tool use, and includes no explicit computation cost. It can therefore reward unnecessary tool calls on already-solvable examples. The claimed learning of tool necessity requires stronger counterfactual evaluation and reward ablations.

The evaluation metrics have important validity gaps. 'Joint accuracy' incorporates partial credit for supposedly safer speed predictions, despite initially being defined as exact matching; slowing or stopping is not universally safer. Strict accuracy should be reported separately. The Gemini-based H-Score lacks a reproducible judging rubric, normalization details, and human validation, limiting conclusions about reasoning quality, comfort, and safety.

All experiments use one dataset and a random 1,500-sample test split, without documenting separation by drive, route, or recording session. There is no external generalization evaluation or closed-loop safety assessment. Four discrete future actions demonstrate sequence prediction, but do not establish improved operational safety or reliable long-horizon planning.

The visual-removal ablation demonstrates sensitivity to missing images, not faithful grounding or robustness. Removing all images is a substantial distribution shift, and a larger performance drop does not rule out textual shortcuts. Counterfactual scene edits, mismatched-image tests, and corrupted-tool evaluations would provide stronger evidence. Controls with passive access to equivalent high-resolution and historical information are also missing.

Novelty and causal attribution remain insufficiently established. The approach primarily combines existing tool-augmented reasoning, mode-conditioned GRPO sampling, and adaptive reasoning selection. Training-stage ablations do not report matched optimization budgets, and there are no individual-tool or reward-component ablations. Consequently, gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed curriculum rather than additional training or richer observations.

Reproducibility is incomplete: RL iteration counts and learning rates, exploration-set size, reward weights and curriculum thresholds, annotation prompts, and evaluation prompts are not provided. Results lack repeated runs or confidence intervals. These omissions are particularly consequential for assessing the small adaptive-mode gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: selectively acquiring additional visual evidence for high-level driving decisions. The integration of text-based reasoning, visual tools, and progressive training is coherent and practically motivated.

The reported improvements are substantial. With tools enabled, DriveAgent-R1 achieves 70.11% first-frame and 44.06% sequence-average scores, compared with 61.42% and 38.03% without tools, and exceeds the evaluated prompted proprietary models on these metrics.

The training-stage ablations, forced-mode evaluations, and separately trained no-tool baseline provide useful evidence that both reinforcement learning and access to visual tools contribute to performance.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish state-of-the-art driving performance or sufficiently isolate methodological novelty. Table 1 compares a task-trained model against one-shot general-purpose VLMs, without adapted driving-specific methods such as AlphaDrive or DriveVLM. The trained no-tool baseline is useful, but matched-compute comparisons against simpler tool-enabled SFT/GRPO pipelines and passive access to equivalent visual information are missing.

The central efficiency claim is untested: there are no latency, token-cost, tool-frequency, or compute measurements. Adaptive selection achieves 44.06% sequence-average accuracy versus 43.20% for forced tool use, while its first-frame score is lower. Without uncertainty estimates and measured savings, this does not establish a compelling advantage over always using tools. The reported 65.93% mode-selection accuracy also lacks constant-policy baselines and oracle-mode class proportions.

The tool reward measures absolute outcome accuracy and call validity, rather than improvement attributable to acquiring information. It can therefore reward unnecessary tool use on already-solvable examples. No ablation of this reward or direct measurement of tool necessity establishes that the selector learns the claimed efficiency–reliability trade-off.

Evaluation is limited to an offline random split of one dataset. Predicting four discrete action pairs over eight seconds does not establish closed-loop safety, long-horizon planning reliability, or robustness to distribution shifts. Per-horizon results, scenario-specific failures, and independent generalization tests are absent; separation by drive or location is also unspecified.

The evaluation metrics need stronger validation. Reported ACC includes partial credit for supposedly safer speed actions, but more deceleration is not universally safer, and strict exact-match results are not provided separately. The Gemini-based H-Score lacks a reproducible judging rubric, normalization details, and human validation, weakening conclusions about reasoning quality, comfort, and safety.

Removing every image demonstrates visual dependence, but does not establish correct grounding or robustness. This intervention changes the input distribution and removes tool evidence simultaneously. Controlled image swaps, misleading tool outputs, individual-tool ablations, and evidence-relevance tests are needed to support the stronger causal claims.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including RL training lengths and learning rates, exploratory-set size, reward weights and curriculum endpoints, annotation thresholds, and baseline/evaluator prompts. No repeated-run variability is reported. These omissions also prevent checking whether the full three-stage pipeline benefits from additional training budget rather than its proposed curriculum.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: acquiring additional visual evidence selectively for high-level driving decisions. The integration of view retrieval, image crops, depth estimation, and object detection provides a concrete implementation.

The progressive training strategy is plausible and supported by useful ablations, including single-stage RL variants matched for training epochs. Cascaded training improves sequence accuracy on both the internal dataset and nuScenes.

Cross-dataset evaluation on nuScenes provides encouraging evidence of transfer: the model achieves 47.10% sequence accuracy versus 44.43% in forced-text mode and 45.14% for the evaluated GPT-5 configuration.
The appendix supplies tool interfaces, labeling rules, prompts, reward formulations, and a useful failure case in which additional visual evidence causes an incorrect decision.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not substantiate the central claims about driving proficiency and safety. It measures offline agreement with discretized recorded actions, without closed-loop execution, collision rates, traffic-rule compliance, or downstream planner integration. The relaxed metric also awards credit for supposedly safer speed predictions without establishing that these actions are safer in context. Strict accuracy and safety-oriented evaluation are needed.

The comparisons are insufficient to establish competitiveness with existing driving methods. Table 1 primarily compares the extensively domain-trained model against general VLMs using one-shot prompts, with closed models restricted to 'no-thinking' configurations. Relevant driving approaches such as Drive-R1, AlphaDrive, and AgentThink are cited but not evaluated. The human comparison uses three drivers viewing only a front image, speed, and navigation, whereas the agent can access additional views and history; this does not establish human-level driving proficiency.

The novelty is insufficiently distinguished from prior work on tool-augmented driving reasoning, visual tool-use RL, and hybrid reasoning. In particular, the cited AgentThink warrants a direct methodological comparison. MP-GRPO mainly enforces balanced mode sampling before standard pooled reward normalization, and the experiments do not isolate this mechanism from simpler balanced-sampling or alternative routing approaches.

The deployment claim is substantially stronger than the efficiency evidence. Mean inference latency is 6.74 seconds on an H20 GPU, exceeding the two-second action interval and consuming much of the eight-second prediction horizon. The paper does not establish how this delay would be accommodated, clearly account for auxiliary tool-model execution and memory, or report tail latency and a forced-text latency baseline. The 3B parameter count describes the agent rather than the complete perception system.

Reproducibility and data independence remain unclear. Training depends on proprietary driving clips and 530K generated VQA pairs, without a stated release plan or sufficient detail to reconstruct the data. Clip-level separation between training and the randomly sampled internal test instances, and separation from domain-alignment images, are not explicitly established. Important optimization settings and several filtering and reward hyperparameters are also unspecified or presented only as examples.

Several central gains are small and lack uncertainty estimates despite stochastic evaluation at temperature 0.7. On Drive-Internal, adaptive selection improves over forced-tool inference by only 0.45 points, and cascaded training exceeds two epochs of FCM-RL by 0.51 points. Training seeds, evaluation repetitions, and confidence intervals are needed. Figure 4 also reports 39.83% after SFT, whereas Table 4 reports 40.88% for the corresponding adaptive variant, without explanation.

The mechanistic evidence is weaker than claimed. Removing images demonstrates input dependence but does not establish faithful visual reasoning or rule out textual shortcuts. The claimed equal-information comparison with Passive-SV is unclear because Retrieve View can access five seconds of history. Mode Selection Accuracy lacks explicit tie handling and sampling details, and the paper provides neither tool-specific ablations nor quantitative tool-use statistics to explain which tools and routing decisions drive the gains.

strengths: The problem is relevant: selectively acquiring additional visual evidence could improve the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff of VLM-based driving behavior prediction. The toolkit and adaptive reasoning modes form a coherent system.

The experiments provide positive evidence of transfer: despite planning training using only Drive-Internal, the model achieves 47.10% sequence-average joint accuracy on nuScenes, compared with 45.14% for the reported GPT-5 baseline.

The paper includes useful ablations on domain alignment, passive versus active perception, and training stages, including controls matched by total RL epochs. The appendix documents tool interfaces, labeling rules, reward construction, and a failure case.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not substantiate the broad safety and human-driving-proficiency claims. It measures offline agreement with automatically discretized recorded trajectories, with no closed-loop execution, collision metrics, traffic-rule evaluation, or validation of the resulting behavior. Multiple safe plans can disagree with a recorded trajectory. Relaxed scoring also assumes slower actions are safer without establishing that assumption in context.

The main comparisons omit specialized driving methods discussed in the paper, such as AlphaDrive and Drive-R1. General-purpose models receive one-shot prompting, while the proposed model receives substantial domain alignment and task-specific training; closed models additionally run in 'no-thinking' mode. These results establish performance under the chosen protocol, but do not adequately establish superiority over competitive driving approaches.

The human comparison is particularly limited. Three drivers label disjoint subsets using only a front-view image, speed, and navigation, whereas the agent can access additional views, historical frames, and perception tools. There is no inter-rater agreement or repeated annotation. Matching these restricted annotation scores does not demonstrate human-level driving proficiency.

The evidence isolating the central innovations is incomplete. MP-GRPO largely combines forced balanced sampling with shared GRPO reward normalization, but there is no direct comparison against separate within-mode normalization or an ablation of the tool-usage reward. The claimed information-matched active/passive comparison also needs clarification: Retrieve View supports five seconds of history, while Passive-SV is described as receiving six views.

Several central gains are modest and lack uncertainty estimates. On Drive-Internal, cascaded RL improves sequence accuracy by only 0.51 points over two epochs of FCM-RL, and adaptive selection improves by 0.45 points over forced tool use. Evaluation uses temperature 0.7 without reported repeated accuracy runs or confidence intervals. MSA also lacks tie-handling details and an always-select-the-better-fixed-mode baseline.

Deployment claims are overstated. Average inference latency is 6.74 seconds on an H20 GPU, despite predictions being spaced at two-second intervals. The paper demonstrates a relative latency reduction, but provides no asynchronous control architecture or closed-loop evidence showing that this delay is usable. It is also unclear whether latency fully includes external perception-tool execution; the 3B parameter claim excludes those auxiliary models.

Reproducibility and benchmark validity remain insufficiently established. Training depends on private driving data and a 530K-pair alignment corpus, with no stated release plan or complete optimization configuration. Clip-level separation between training and testing, and overlap with alignment data, are not clearly documented. Automatically refined labels receive no reported independent human audit. Finally, removing all images demonstrates visual dependence, but does not establish faithful reasoning or eliminate textual shortcuts.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: selectively acquiring additional visual evidence for high-level driving decisions. The integration of visual tools, adaptive mode selection, and progressive training forms a coherent system.

The training ablations include useful controls with matched total RL epochs and show consistent benefits on both datasets. On nuScenes, cascaded training achieves 47.10% sequence accuracy versus 44.60% and 43.57% for the two single-stage alternatives.

Cross-dataset evaluation on nuScenes provides encouraging evidence of transfer beyond Drive-Internal. The trained 3B model also benefits more consistently from tool access than the untrained small-model baselines.

The appendix provides tool interfaces, data-generation procedures, reward definitions, and qualitative examples, including a useful failure analysis showing how additional views can introduce misleading evidence.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish the central claims about safer driving or human-level driving proficiency. It measures offline agreement with automatically discretized recorded trajectories, without closed-loop execution, collision metrics, or safety-critical scenario analysis. The relaxed metric awards partial credit for slower actions without demonstrating that they are safer in context; strict accuracy and per-action results are needed.

The human and frontier-model comparisons are limited. Three drivers each label disjoint subsets using only the front image, speed, and navigation, while the agent can access additional views, historical frames, and perception tools. There is no inter-rater analysis. Closed models are evaluated in 'no-thinking' mode, so the results do not establish parity with their strongest reasoning configurations.

Evidence isolating the methodological contribution remains incomplete. There are no direct comparisons with specialized driving VLMs or simpler learned routing strategies, and no ablation isolating the contrastive tool reward or the group-normalization design. MP-GRPO primarily modifies rollout allocation within GRPO; its distinct advantage over simpler alternatives is not established.

Several key gains are modest and lack uncertainty estimates despite stochastic evaluation at temperature 0.7. Adaptive mode improves over forced-tool mode by only 0.45 points on Drive-Internal and 0.72 points on nuScenes. Training seeds, confidence intervals, and repeated accuracy evaluations are absent. MSA also lacks a clear treatment of ties and sampling variability.

The active-versus-passive comparison needs tighter information controls. Retrieve View supports five seconds of historical imagery, whereas Passive-SV is described as receiving six views; it is unclear whether history is disabled for the claimed identical-information comparison. Removing images demonstrates visual dependence, but does not establish faithful reasoning or eliminate textual shortcuts.

Deployment claims exceed the efficiency evidence. Average inference takes 6.74 seconds on an H20 GPU for predictions spaced two seconds apart. The paper does not demonstrate how this delay is accommodated by a driving system, clearly account for external-tool execution costs, or report tail latency and a forced-text latency baseline.

Reproducibility and data validity remain unresolved. Training depends on private driving and VQA data, with insufficient detail on clip-level train/test separation and overlap with domain-alignment images. Automated label refinement lacks a human quality audit, and important optimization settings and exact filtering thresholds are missing. These gaps, together with the evaluation limitations, leave the paper below the acceptance threshold despite its promising system design.
